title: Gena Playing Hanoi
directAnswer: This is Towers of Hanoi with FOUR pegs, asking for the minimum number of legal moves to gather all disks onto the first peg from an arbitrary start. Because there's no neat closed form for 4 pegs, model each configuration as a node: encode the whole tower as a base-4 number (2 bits per disk = which of the 4 pegs it sits on). Run BFS from the start state to the all-on-peg-1 goal — BFS over an unweighted state graph gives the minimum move count directly. With n ≤ 10 disks there are at most 4¹⁰ ≈ 1.05M states, each with ≤ 12 candidate moves, so plain BFS is fast. O(4ⁿ · pegs²) time and O(4ⁿ) space.

remember.pattern: Shortest path in an implicit state graph → BFS over encoded configurations
rules: The **top** disk of a peg is its **smallest** disk; only the top may move.
A move is legal only onto an **empty peg** or onto a **larger** disk — never a smaller one.
Encode the configuration as **2 bits per disk** (peg 0–3); the full state is a single integer in [0, 4ⁿ).
Use **BFS**, not DFS — BFS on an unweighted graph yields the minimum number of moves; DFS does not.
Mark states **visited** (dist array) so you never re-expand — without it the search cycles forever (move a disk back and forth).
whenToUse: Minimum moves / steps between configurations under discrete legal transitions
State space is finite and modest enough to enumerate (here ≤ 4¹⁰)
Each configuration encodes compactly into an integer or tuple
Transitions are reversible and unweighted → shortest path = fewest moves
antiSignals: Classic 3-peg Hanoi from one peg to another → closed form 2ⁿ − 1, no search needed
State space explodes beyond memory (huge n, many pegs) → IDA*/meet-in-the-middle, not plain BFS
Moves have varying costs → Dijkstra, not BFS
You only need feasibility, not the minimum → DFS/union-find may suffice
remember.takeaway: When a puzzle asks for the fewest moves and the configurations are enumerable, treat each configuration as a graph node and BFS. The whole craft is a compact state encoding (base-4 integer here) plus a correct legal-move generator — the shortest-path machinery is standard.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that 4-peg Hanoi has no clean formula and reframe 'minimum moves' as BFS shortest path over an encoded state space, with a correct legal-move generator and a visited set.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reaching for a closed-form Frame–Stewart-style formula (it doesn't apply to an arbitrary start), using DFS (won't give the minimum), or omitting the visited set so the search cycles.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the 2-bits-per-disk encoding, explain why the top disk is the smallest, generate moves correctly, and mention bidirectional BFS or A* with an admissible heuristic to shrink the explored frontier.

problemStatement:
Gena has a Towers of Hanoi setup with **4 pegs** and `n` disks of distinct sizes (disk 1 is the smallest, disk `n` the largest). You're given the starting peg of each disk in an arbitrary (but legal) configuration.

As in standard Hanoi, you may move the **topmost** disk of any peg onto another peg, but only if the destination peg is empty or its top disk is **larger** than the one being moved. Find the **minimum number of moves** required to stack all `n` disks onto **peg 1**.
constraints: Disk i has size i; only the smallest disk on a peg (its top) can be moved
A disk may be placed only on an empty peg or on a strictly larger disk
The starting configuration is legal; goal is all disks on peg 1
understanding: Each disk independently sits on one of four pegs, so a configuration is fully described by the peg of every disk — a vector that packs into a base-4 integer. Legal moves connect configurations: from any peg, lift its smallest disk and drop it on a peg whose current top is bigger (or which is empty). Every move costs 1, so the minimum move count from start to the all-on-peg-1 state is exactly the shortest-path distance in this graph — the textbook job of breadth-first search.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many pegs — 3 or 4?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Four. That's the whole twist: 3-peg Hanoi has the closed form 2ⁿ−1, but 4 pegs (and an arbitrary start) have no simple formula, so we search.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which peg is the destination, and what's the start?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: All disks must end on peg 1. The start is an arbitrary legal placement given as input — not necessarily all on one peg.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I move any disk, or only the top of a peg?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only the top (smallest) disk of a peg, and only onto an empty peg or a larger disk — standard Hanoi legality.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is n, and does the state space fit in memory?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: n ≤ 10, so at most 4¹⁰ ≈ 1.05M states. A flat int/byte array of that size for distances fits comfortably, making plain BFS viable.

examples.explanation: The single disk is on peg 4; one move puts it on peg 1.
Both disks already on peg 1 — the start equals the goal, zero moves.
Disk 1 on peg 2, disk 2 on peg 3. Move disk 2 (peg 3 → peg 1, empty), then disk 1 (peg 2 → peg 1, onto the larger disk 2). Two moves.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Unbounded DFS Over Move Sequences
approaches.whenToMention: State it to expose why naive search fails (cycles, no shortest guarantee), motivating BFS with a visited set.
hints: From a configuration, enumerate every legal move and recurse on the resulting configuration, tracking the move count.
Without remembering visited configurations you can move a disk back and forth forever — the search may never terminate.
Even bounding the depth (iterative deepening) explores an exponential tree because the same configuration is reached along many paths.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each state has up to 12 move candidates; a depth-d DFS explores up to 12^d sequences, and without a visited set it revisits configurations endlessly, so it neither terminates reliably nor guarantees the minimum.
approaches.explanation:
The literal interpretation: try moves recursively and keep the best total found.

**Why it's broken as written.** Moves are reversible — you can shift a disk to another peg and immediately shift it back — so a depth-first walk can loop indefinitely. Even if you cap the depth (iterative deepening DFS), the configuration graph has many paths into the same node, so you re-explore states exponentially.

**Why DFS can't give the minimum cheaply.** DFS dives down one branch fully before trying others, so the first time it reaches the goal need not be via the fewest moves. You'd have to explore *all* paths up to the optimal depth and take the minimum — exactly the exponential blow-up.

**What the failure teaches.** Two fixes are needed: (1) never re-expand a configuration (a visited set), and (2) explore in order of increasing move count so the first time you touch the goal is optimal. Doing both *is* breadth-first search — the next approach.
approaches.insight: Reversible moves turn naive DFS into an infinite walk, and DFS's depth-first order breaks the 'first hit is optimal' property. Recognising both flaws points straight at BFS with a visited set as the right tool.

approaches.name: BFS Over Base-4 Encoded States (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'encode each tower as a base-4 integer and BFS from start to the all-on-peg-1 goal'.
hints: Encode the configuration: 2 bits per disk hold its peg (0–3). The whole state is one integer in [0, 4ⁿ).
To generate moves, find each peg's top disk (its smallest disk), then try dropping it on any peg that's empty or has a larger top.
BFS from the start integer; the first time you dequeue the goal (all disks on peg 1, encoded 0) its distance is the minimum move count.
approaches.complexityReasoning: At most 4ⁿ states; each is expanded once and generates ≤ 4·3 = 12 moves, each found in O(n) (scanning disks for tops). So time is O(4ⁿ · n) (≈ O(4ⁿ · pegs²) treating peg work as constant), and the distance array is O(4ⁿ) space.
approaches.explanation:
Model configurations as graph nodes and run breadth-first search.

**Encoding.** Disk `i`'s peg is stored in bits `2i..2i+1` of an integer `state`. With `n ≤ 10`, `state` fits in 20 bits; the full state space is `[0, 4ⁿ)`. The goal — every disk on peg 1 — encodes as `0` (peg index 0).

**Finding tops.** The movable disk on a peg is its **smallest** disk. Scan disks from largest to smallest, recording each disk's peg; the last write per peg leaves the smallest disk index, i.e. that peg's top. A peg with no disk has no top.

**Generating moves.** For each peg `from` with top disk `d`, and each other peg `to`: the move is legal if `to` is empty or its top disk is **larger** than `d` (a larger disk index). Apply it by rewriting `d`'s two bits to `to`, producing the neighbour state.

**Why BFS is exactly right.** Every move costs 1, so the graph is unweighted; BFS visits states in non-decreasing distance order, guaranteeing the first time the goal is reached uses the fewest moves. A `dist` array doubles as the visited set: only relax a neighbour whose distance is still unset.

**Cost.** Each of the ≤ 4ⁿ states is expanded once with O(n) work to find tops and ≤ 12 neighbours, so the search is linear in the state-space size — about 12 million elementary steps at n = 10, which is fast.
approaches.insight: The entire problem reduces to two design choices: a compact, collision-free state encoding (2 bits per disk) and a correct legal-move generator (top = smallest, destination must be larger or empty). Once those are right, BFS is boilerplate and the minimum is whatever distance the goal gets.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def gena(self, n: int, posts: list[int]) -> int:
    start = 0
    for i in range(n):
        start |= (posts[i] - 1) << (2 * i)
    total = 1 << (2 * n)
    dist = [-1] * total
    dist[start] = 0
    q = deque([start])
    GOAL = 0  # all disks on peg 0 (peg 1)
    while q:
        state = q.popleft()
        if state == GOAL:
            return dist[state]
        top = [-1, -1, -1, -1]
        for d in range(n - 1, -1, -1):           # large→small: smallest disk wins as top
            peg = (state >> (2 * d)) & 3
            top[peg] = d
        for frm in range(4):
            d = top[frm]
            if d < 0:
                continue
            for to in range(4):
                if to == frm:
                    continue
                if top[to] == -1 or top[to] > d:  # empty or larger top
                    nxt = (state & ~(3 << (2 * d))) | (to << (2 * d))
                    if dist[nxt] == -1:
                        dist[nxt] = dist[state] + 1
                        q.append(nxt)
    return dist[GOAL]

approaches.name: Bidirectional BFS
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the frontier-shrinking refinement: search from both start and goal and meet in the middle.
hints: Run two BFS frontiers simultaneously — one from the start, one from the goal — and stop when they touch.
Moves are reversible, so the goal-side search uses the same move generator; the meeting distance is the sum of the two depths.
Always expand the smaller frontier next to keep both shallow; the explored region is roughly two radius-(d/2) balls instead of one radius-d ball.
approaches.complexityReasoning: If the optimal distance is d, unidirectional BFS explores ~b^d states; meeting in the middle explores ~2·b^(d/2), an exponential reduction in the explored frontier (b = branching factor).
approaches.explanation:
Plain BFS already fits in memory for n ≤ 10, but bidirectional BFS dramatically shrinks the *explored* frontier when the optimal depth is large.

**Idea.** Because every move is reversible, a path from start to goal is also a path from goal to start. So grow two BFS frontiers — `distF` from the start and `distB` from the goal — alternating, always expanding whichever frontier currently has fewer nodes. The moment a state has been reached from both sides, the answer is `distF[state] + distB[state]`; take the minimum over all such meeting states discovered at the touching layer.

**Why it's faster.** A single BFS to depth `d` touches on the order of `b^d` states. Two searches to depth `d/2` each touch `b^(d/2)`, and `2·b^(d/2) ≪ b^d`. For deep optimal solutions this is the difference between exploring most of the million states and exploring a small fraction.

**Caveats.** It's more code (two visited maps, careful meeting check) and the same worst-case memory. Reach for it only when the unidirectional frontier is genuinely large; for small n the plain BFS is cleaner and plenty fast.
approaches.insight: Reversibility is the enabler: it lets the goal-side search reuse the exact move generator, so meeting in the middle converts one deep search into two shallow ones — an exponential cut in explored states for deep instances.

commonMistakes: Trying to apply a closed-form Hanoi formula — none exists for 4 pegs from an arbitrary start.
Using DFS instead of BFS, so the first goal hit isn't the minimum.
Omitting the visited/dist guard, causing infinite cycling on reversible moves.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Top disk taken as the largest
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only the smallest disk on a peg is on top and movable. Treating the largest as the top generates illegal moves and corrupts the search.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: for (int d = 0; d < n; d++) top[(state >> (2*d)) & 3] = d;  // smallest overwritten → top becomes LARGEST
commonMistakesDetailed.good: for (int d = n - 1; d >= 0; d--) top[(state >> (2*d)) & 3] = d;  // smallest disk ends as top

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Placing a disk on a smaller one
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A move is legal only onto an empty peg or a larger disk. Dropping a bigger disk onto a smaller one violates Hanoi rules and yields impossible configurations.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if to != frm:  # forgot the size check
    nxt = move(state, d, to)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if to != frm and (top[to] == -1 or top[to] > d):
    nxt = move(state, d, to)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: DFS instead of BFS
commonMistakesDetailed.why: DFS explores depth-first, so the first time it reaches the goal is not necessarily via the fewest moves; you'd have to exhaust all paths. BFS visits by increasing distance, making the first goal hit optimal.

patternNote: Minimum-moves puzzles over enumerable configurations are shortest-path problems: encode each configuration as an integer, generate legal transitions, and BFS from start to goal. Bidirectional BFS or A* with an admissible heuristic trims the frontier when the optimal depth is large. Same template as Sliding Puzzle and Open the Lock.
